raw_case_text:
A 49-year-old male with a medical history significant for previous intravenous (IV) methamphetamine use, active tobacco use, and Neisseria meningitidis bacteremia and meningitis (four months prior) was transferred to our facility for concerns of acute hemoptysis with pulmonary infiltrates. Before admission, the patient was seen at an outside hospital (OSH) and treated for an acute septic shock with chief complaints of nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Vitals revealed hypotension of 85/40 mmHg, bradycardia of 58 beats/min, a temperature of 97.5 F, and a respiratory rate of 18 breaths/minute. OSH labs demonstrated leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, elevated creatinine, and hypoalbuminemia (Table 1). Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated gastroenteritis and right-sided colitis. Initial blood cultures grew gram-negative coccobacilli, and the patient was started on IV vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam. He did not respond to fluid resuscitation and was started on vasopressors. The stool workup was positive for C. difficile colitis, and he was switched to oral vancomycin with improvement. The hospital course revealed septic shock resolution but was complicated by hemoptysis and a follow-up chest x-ray displaying pulmonary infiltrates. He was then transferred to our facility's medical intensive care unit for further evaluation. Upon arrival, he denied chest pain, palpitations, abdominal pain, fever, or chills. He affirmed productive cough (brown-colored phlegm) with dyspnea.
Clinical examination revealed him to be awake, alert, and well-oriented to time, place, and person with no focal neurological deficits. He had poor overall hygiene, extensive dental caries, regular heart rate and rhythm, and a grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur best heard over the left fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line. Breath sounds were reduced bilaterally on the anterior chest fields, with rales appreciable in the upper and lower lung fields on auscultation. The abdomen was diffusely tender but not distended, and the extremities revealed no abnormalities. Labs revealed leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, elevated creatinine, elevated inflammatory markers, elevated NT-proBNP, hypocomplementemia, nonreactive syphilis, human immunodeficiency virus, and acute viral hepatitis serology (Table 2). Although Antinuclear Antibody (ANA) was elevated, the lupus serology was negative without vasculitis or other autoimmune manifestations; his hemoptysis and creatinine elevation resolved spontaneously without steroids, making Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated disease less likely. Chest x-ray demonstrated extensive patchy bilateral areas of airspace opacification (Fig. 1). CT scan of the chest with IV contrast displayed multifocal innumerable upper lobe predominant ground glass and nodular opacity in bronchovascular distribution and enlarged mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes (Fig. 2). OSH-positive blood culture samples were sent to the state microbiology laboratory and were confirmed positive for beta-lactamase-negative NTHI (Table 2).
The infectious disease (ID) team was consulted for NTHI bacteremia. Antimicrobials were de-escalated to piperacillin-tazobactam for NTHI bacteremia and oral vancomycin for C. difficile colitis. As the chest x-ray revealed widespread pulmonary airspace opacities, a trans-thoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was ordered due to an IE concern. TTE demonstrated a normal ejection fraction, no wall motion abnormalities, and a 1.5 cm vegetation over the anterior mitral valve (MV) leaflet. A trans-esophageal echocardiogram (TEE) confirmed large mobile vegetation (1.73 x 0.55 cm) visualized on the atrial aspect of the anterior leaflet of the MV, which protruded to the left ventricle during diastole with severe mitral regurgitation (Fig. 3 & 4). After TEE confirmed IE, a panoramic x-ray of the oral cavity revealed multiple fractured maxillary teeth with extensive dental caries addressed by surgical extraction and alveoloplasty in all four quadrants. Based on ID team recommendations, IV ceftriaxone 2 gm every 24 h was started, and piperacillin-tazobactam was stopped. Cardiothoracic surgery (CTS) was consulted, and the patient underwent a bioprosthetic mitral valve replacement (MVR). Mitral valve histopathology revealed acute inflammation and necrosis consistent with IE. The patient completed six weeks of ceftriaxone inpatient after the MVR and was free of symptoms with a repeat chest x-ray revealing no acute cardiopulmonary abnormalities at a two-week CTS clinic follow-up. He was referred to a tertiary center for additional evaluation of his hypocomplementemia.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 49-year-old male was transferred to the medical intensive care unit with acute hemoptysis, productive cough with brown phlegm, dyspnea, and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Prior to transfer, the patient had presented to an outside hospital with nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and septic shock (BP 85/40 mmHg, HR 58 bpm, temperature 97.5 °F, RR 18/min), where he had gram-negative coccobacilli bacteremia and Clostridium difficile colitis treated with vasopressors, IV vancomycin, piperacillin/tazobactam, and subsequently oral vancomycin. Although his septic shock resolved, his course was complicated by acute hemoptysis and new pulmonary infiltrates on chest radiograph, prompting transfer to our medical ICU.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of prior intravenous methamphetamine use, active tobacco use, and Neisseria meningitidis bacteremia and meningitis 4 months prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: On arrival at the receiving facility, positive for productive cough with brown-colored phlegm and dyspnea; negative for chest pain, palpitations, abdominal pain, fever, or chills.

objective.physical_examination: Awake, alert, and oriented to person, place, and time without focal neurological deficits. General examination showed poor hygiene and extensive dental caries. Cardiovascular examination revealed regular rate and rhythm with a grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur best heard at the left fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line. Pulmonary auscultation showed bilaterally reduced anterior breath sounds with upper and lower lung field rales. Abdomen was diffusely tender without distension; extremities were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Outside hospital labs showed leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, elevated creatinine, and hypoalbuminemia. Receiving facility labs demonstrated leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, elevated creatinine, elevated inflammatory markers, elevated NT-proBNP, hypocomplementemia, elevated ANA (with negative lupus-specific serologies), and nonreactive HIV, syphilis, and acute viral hepatitis serologies. Chest X-ray showed extensive patchy bilateral airspace opacification. Panoramic oral X-ray showed multiple fractured maxillary teeth and extensive dental caries.
objective.advanced_workup: Outside hospital abdominal/pelvic CT showed gastroenteritis and right-sided colitis. Chest CT with IV contrast demonstrated innumerable multifocal upper-lobe-predominant ground-glass and nodular opacities in a bronchovascular distribution along with enlarged mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes. Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) showed normal ejection fraction, no wall motion abnormalities, and a 1.5 cm anterior mitral valve leaflet vegetation. Transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) confirmed a large mobile vegetation (1.73 x 0.55 cm) on the atrial aspect of the anterior mitral valve leaflet prolapsing into the left ventricle during diastole with severe mitral regurgitation. Mitral valve histopathology following surgical replacement demonstrated acute inflammation and necrosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Beta-lactamase-negative non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae (NTHI) bacteremia and native mitral valve infective endocarditis with severe mitral regurgitation and septic pulmonary emboli, alongside resolving Clostridium difficile colitis, in an HIV-negative 49-year-old male (confirmed by state microbiology laboratory identification of NTHI from outside blood cultures and TEE/histopathology confirmation of mitral valve endocarditis; SLE and ANCA-associated vasculitis were excluded). Treatment included antimicrobial de-escalation to IV ceftriaxone 2 g every 24 hours (with oral vancomycin for C. difficile), four-quadrant dental extraction and alveoloplasty, and bioprosthetic mitral valve replacement (MVR) followed by a 6-week inpatient course of IV ceftriaxone. At 2-week cardiothoracic surgery follow-up, he was asymptomatic with a clear repeat chest radiograph and was referred to a tertiary center for evaluation of persistent hypocomplementemia.
